title: Policies for information security
description: Define, approve, publish, and review IS policies

title: Information security roles and responsibilities
description: Assign and communicate IS roles across the organisation

title: Segregation of duties
description: Separate conflicting duties to reduce fraud and error risk
question: Is there any single person in your team who can make a change, approve it, and deploy it all by themselves — with no one else checking?
intent: This is a check-and-balance control. The goal is to prevent any one person from being able to cause harm — intentionally or accidentally — without another set of eyes. Think of it like requiring two keys to open a safe.
examples: Requiring a different person to approve a pull request than the one who wrote the code
Separating who can raise a payment from who can approve it in your finance workflow
Using a 4-eyes approval step in your deployment pipeline
Making sure the person who can create accounts isn't the same one who reviews the access log

title: Management responsibilities
description: Require managers to actively enforce IS policies

title: Contact with authorities
description: Maintain contacts with law enforcement and relevant regulators

title: Contact with special interest groups
description: Maintain contacts with security forums and professional bodies

title: Threat intelligence
description: Collect, analyse, and act on information about current IS threats

title: Information security in project management
description: Address IS requirements in all project management activities

title: Inventory of information and other assets
description: Identify all information assets and assign clear ownership
question: Could you quickly list every component of your service — servers, databases, APIs, third-party tools — and say who's responsible for each one?
intent: You can't protect what you don't know you have. This is about keeping an accurate picture of everything that makes up your service — infrastructure, data stores, integrations, and the people accountable for them.
examples: A CMDB or spreadsheet listing all VMs, containers, databases, and SaaS tools your service uses
Tags applied to all cloud resources with owner and service name
A network or architecture diagram that's kept up to date
A list of all third-party integrations and what data they handle

title: Acceptable use of information and other assets
description: Define rules for acceptable use of all information assets

title: Return of assets
description: Ensure assets are returned when employment ends or roles change

title: Classification of information
description: Classify information based on legal requirements, value, and sensitivity

title: Labelling of information
description: Apply labels to information according to the classification scheme
question: Does your system tag or mark the data it handles so people know how sensitive it is — for example in document headers, file names, or database fields?
intent: Labels help people handle data correctly. Without them, a confidential document might get forwarded to the wrong distribution list simply because nobody knew it was sensitive. Labelling is the link between the classification policy and how data actually gets treated day to day.
examples: Document templates with classification headers and footers (e.g. "INTERNAL USE ONLY")
Metadata fields populated when creating records in your CMS or data platform
Automated sensitivity labels in Microsoft 365 Purview or Google Workspace
Database columns flagged as containing PII in your schema documentation

title: Information transfer
description: Define rules and controls for transferring information between parties
question: When data leaves your service — through an API, a file export, or an email — is it encrypted and heading only to places it's supposed to go?
intent: Data in transit is vulnerable. Every time data moves — between systems, to a third party, or into a partner's hands — there's a risk it's intercepted or ends up somewhere unintended. This control is about making transfer channels secure and intentional.
examples: Enforcing TLS on all API endpoints (no plain HTTP)
Using SFTP or secure file transfer instead of FTP for batch transfers
Requiring that data shared with partners goes through an approved integration, not a personal email attachment
API gateway policies that reject requests from unlisted consumer systems

title: Access control
description: Define and implement access control rules based on business and security needs
question: Does each person — and each connected system — only have access to the parts of your service they actually need for their job?
intent: Limiting who can see or do what in your system reduces the blast radius when credentials are stolen or someone acts in bad faith. The fewer things an account can do, the less damage it can cause.
examples: RBAC with clearly defined roles (viewer, editor, admin) and no catch-all "super user" role
Separate service accounts for each integration with only the permissions that integration needs
Access controlled by team membership in your identity provider
Regular review where managers confirm who in their team still needs what access

title: Identity management
description: Manage the full lifecycle of all identities (create, update, disable, delete)
question: Do you have a clear process for giving someone access when they join, updating it when they change roles, and removing it promptly when they leave?
intent: Orphaned accounts — especially admin ones belonging to people who have left — are one of the most common and avoidable security risks. This is about keeping your user directory accurate and current.
examples: Automated provisioning and deprovisioning tied to your HR system
SSO so there's one place to disable all access when someone leaves
Quarterly access reviews where managers confirm their team's access is still correct
Service accounts tied to a team or system, not an individual

title: Authentication information
description: Control how authentication credentials are allocated, managed, and used
question: Are all accounts in your system protected with strong authentication — and do you have a clear process for what happens when a credential is shared, reset, or compromised?
intent: Weak or shared passwords remain one of the most common ways services get breached. This control is about making sure credentials are strong, private, and handled securely — not emailed around, written on whiteboards, or reused across services.
examples: MFA enforced for all users, especially admins
No shared service accounts — every person has a named account
Service accounts using managed identities or certificates rather than static passwords
An automated alert when there are multiple failed login attempts on the same account
A clear process for rotating credentials when someone with access leaves the team

title: Access rights
description: Provision, review, modify, and remove access rights throughout their lifecycle
question: When someone moves to a different team or leaves the organisation, how quickly do their access rights get updated — and is there someone who checks that this actually happened?
intent: Access that's never removed accumulates over time. People end up with permissions from three previous roles and nobody notices. This control is about making the lifecycle of access rights explicit — not just granting access but also taking it back.
examples: A Joiner/Mover/Leaver workflow integrated with HR triggers
Automated revocation when an HR termination record is created
Access recertification campaign every 6 months where managers approve or revoke
Timestamped records of when access was granted and removed

title: Information security in supplier relationships
description: Define IS requirements for all supplier and third-party relationships

title: Addressing IS within supplier agreements
description: Include IS requirements in all supplier contracts

title: Managing IS in the ICT supply chain
description: Monitor and manage IS risks in the ICT supply chain
question: Do you know which third-party tools, open-source libraries, or cloud services your system depends on — and have you checked whether they're actually trustworthy?
intent: Your service is only as secure as its weakest dependency. When a component you rely on is compromised — like the Log4Shell vulnerability — you need to know you're affected and be able to act fast. Most teams have far more dependencies than they realise.
examples: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) listing all third-party components
Automated dependency scanning via tools like Dependabot, Snyk, or OWASP Dependency-Check
A documented list of third-party SaaS tools your service relies on, with DPAs in place
A process for monitoring security advisories for your key dependencies

title: Monitoring and review of supplier services
description: Regularly review and audit supplier service delivery and security posture

title: Information security for use of cloud services
description: Manage IS for cloud service acquisition, use, configuration, and exit
question: For each cloud service your system uses, do you know what data goes into it, who can access it, how it's configured — and what happens if you need to leave that provider?
intent: Cloud services are often added quickly without thinking through the security implications. Once data is in a cloud service you didn't properly evaluate, it's hard to get it back under control. This is about being intentional: knowing what you're using, how it's configured, and that you could exit safely if needed.
examples: A cloud asset inventory with security baseline checked for each service
MFA and strong IAM enforced on all cloud management consoles
Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tool like Defender for Cloud or AWS Security Hub
Documented exit strategy per critical cloud provider
Data residency and processing location confirmed in provider agreements

title: IS incident management planning and preparation
description: Plan and prepare for IS incident management processes and procedures

title: Assessment and decision on IS events
description: Assess IS events and classify them as incidents when appropriate

title: Response to information security incidents
description: Respond to IS incidents following documented procedures

title: Learning from information security incidents
description: Use knowledge from incidents to strengthen controls and prevent recurrence

title: Collection of evidence
description: Procedures for identifying, collecting, and preserving evidence

title: Information security during disruption
description: Plan for maintaining IS controls during and after significant disruptions
question: If something went wrong and your service had to run in emergency or degraded mode, would your security controls still be in place — or would some of them get bypassed?
intent: Under pressure, teams sometimes skip security steps to restore service quickly. This control is a reminder that security shouldn't be the first thing switched off in a crisis. Your minimum security posture needs to hold even when things are hard.
examples: Documented emergency access procedures that still require MFA and logging
Break-glass admin accounts with a mandatory post-use review
Security monitoring and alerting that stays active during failover or maintenance windows
A defined "minimum security baseline" that must be in place even in degraded operation

title: ICT readiness for business continuity
description: Plan, implement, and test ICT continuity to meet business continuity objectives
question: If your service went down tomorrow, do you know how long it would take to get it back up — and have you actually tested that?
intent: Having a backup or recovery plan is only useful if it actually works when you need it. This is about being honest: do you know your recovery time target, is there a tested runbook, and did the last test actually succeed?
examples: Documented RTO (time to restore) and RPO (data loss tolerance) for your service
A tested disaster recovery runbook with step-by-step instructions
Annual DR test with documented results and any gaps tracked to resolution
Runbook stored somewhere accessible even if your primary systems are all down

title: Legal, statutory and regulatory requirements
description: Identify and document all relevant legal and regulatory IS requirements

title: Intellectual property rights
description: Protect intellectual property and comply with all IP-related legal requirements

title: Protection of records
description: Protect records from loss, destruction, falsification, and unauthorised access
question: Are the records your service creates protected from accidental deletion or tampering — and do you know how long you're required to keep them?
intent: Records are often needed for legal, regulatory, or audit purposes long after the fact. If they've been deleted prematurely, corrupted, or can't be proven to be authentic, it can cause serious legal and compliance problems.
examples: Write-once or immutable storage for audit logs
Retention policies configured in your database or document management system
Access controls preventing deletion of records during their retention period
Regular backup of critical records with restore verification

title: Privacy and protection of PII
description: Protect privacy and personally identifiable information per applicable legislation
question: Does your service handle personal data? If so, do you know exactly what data you're holding, why, how long you're keeping it, and who can see it?
intent: Personal data carries legal obligations. This is about being intentional with PII — only collect what you genuinely need, keep it only as long as necessary, protect it properly, and be ready to respond if someone asks you to delete it.
examples: A data inventory showing what PII your service processes and on what legal basis
Privacy notice for users explaining how their data is used
Automated deletion of personal data after the retention period expires
A documented process for responding to Subject Access Requests within 30 days
DPIA completed if your service does high-risk PII processing

title: Independent review of information security
description: Review IS implementation and controls independently at planned intervals

title: Compliance with policies, rules and standards
description: Ensure compliance with IS policies, rules, and standards across the organisation
question: Is there anything in your service that you know isn't following the company's security policies — and if so, is there a documented plan to fix it?
intent: Having policies is only useful if people follow them. This control is about honest self-assessment — are you actually in line with what's expected, and if not, is there a transparent gap with a plan and owner? Undocumented exceptions are a risk in themselves.
examples: Regular self-assessment against your organisation's security baseline
Exceptions formally documented with a risk acceptance, owner, and remediation target date
Automated policy-as-code checks in your cloud environment
Security findings tracked in a backlog with clear owners and due dates

title: Documented operating procedures
description: Document and maintain operating procedures for all IS-relevant activities
question: If you were hit by a bus tomorrow, could someone else on your team run your service securely — using documented procedures rather than tribal knowledge?
intent: Knowledge locked in one person's head is a risk. If that person is unavailable, critical tasks get done inconsistently or not at all. Documented procedures ensure that security-relevant tasks happen correctly regardless of who does them.
examples: Runbooks for patching, deployments, key rotation, and incident response
Onboarding documentation for new team members covering how to access and operate the service securely
Procedures stored in a shared, accessible location — not on one person's local drive
Regular review (at least annually) to keep procedures current

title: Screening
description: Perform background verification checks on all candidates prior to employment

title: Terms and conditions of employment
description: Include IS responsibilities in all employment terms and conditions

title: IS awareness, education and training
description: Provide IS awareness and training for all personnel

title: Disciplinary process
description: Maintain a formal disciplinary process for IS policy violations

title: Responsibilities after termination
description: Define and enforce IS responsibilities that continue after employment ends

title: Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements
description: Require NDAs from all personnel and relevant contractors

title: Remote working
description: Define IS policies and technical controls for remote working arrangements
question: Do you know whether your team members are accessing your service's admin tools or sensitive data from personal devices or unsecured home networks — and what controls are in place if they are?
intent: Remote work expands the attack surface significantly. When people work from home, the protections that exist in the office — controlled network, managed devices, clear desk — often disappear. This is about making sure remote access to your service doesn't create unnecessary risk.
examples: VPN or zero-trust network access required for any production admin activity
MDM enforced on devices used to access production systems
Guidance against using personal devices for production access
Screen lock policy and auto-lock configured on all work devices
No access to production admin consoles from public Wi-Fi without VPN

title: Information security event reporting
description: Require all personnel to report IS events through official channels

title: Physical security perimeters
description: Define and use security perimeters to protect areas containing sensitive assets

title: Physical entry controls
description: Control physical access to secure areas with appropriate authentication

title: Securing offices, rooms and facilities
description: Design and apply physical security measures for all offices and facilities

title: Physical security monitoring
description: Continuously monitor premises for unauthorised physical access

title: Protecting against physical and environmental threats
description: Protect against fire, flood, earthquake, and other environmental threats

title: Working in secure areas
description: Define and enforce procedures for working in high-security areas

title: Clear desk and clear screen
description: Require clear desk and clear screen to be observed at all times

title: Equipment siting and protection
description: Protect equipment from environmental hazards and reduce opportunities for unauthorised access
question: Are the physical servers, network gear, or other hardware used by your service positioned safely — away from hazards like excessive heat, moisture, or areas where they could be seen or accessed by visitors?
intent: Where you put equipment matters. Kit near windows can be seen and targeted. Equipment near water pipes or air conditioning units can be physically damaged. This is about the physical positioning of individual devices, not just the building they're in.
examples: Servers and network equipment mounted in locked racks in secure rooms
Network equipment positioned away from public areas and visitor routes
Equipment not visible through windows or from reception
Environmental sensors (temperature, humidity, water) in server rooms

title: Security of assets off-premises
description: Protect assets and information when used outside organisational premises
question: Are there laptops, drives, or other devices used by your service that leave the office — and are they protected against the risk of being lost or stolen?
intent: The moment a device leaves the building, you lose physical control of it. Encryption and remote wipe are your safety net. Without them, a lost laptop can mean a serious data breach.
examples: Full disk encryption on all laptops (BitLocker, FileVault)
Remote wipe capability enabled and tested
VPN required before any production system access from outside the office
Hardware security tokens (YubiKey) for high-privilege remote access
Clear guidelines on what data should and shouldn't be stored on portable devices

title: Storage media
description: Manage storage media through its full lifecycle: acquisition, use, transport, and disposal
question: Are there any USB drives, backup tapes, or physical hard drives used by your service — and do you know where they are, who has them, and how they get disposed of eventually?
intent: Physical media is easy to lose or steal, and it often bypasses all your digital security controls. A lost unencrypted backup tape can be as damaging as a network breach — and it's often easier for an attacker to just pick one up.
examples: Only encrypted USB drives approved for use
Inventory of all removable media with assigned owner
Secure courier used for any off-site tape or media transport
Certificate of destruction obtained from media disposal vendor
Formal process before any media leaves the building

title: Supporting utilities
description: Protect equipment from power failures and other utility disruptions

title: Cabling security
description: Protect power and communications cables from interception or physical damage
question: Is the network cabling in areas used by your service protected from accidental damage — and could someone plug an unauthorised device into an open port without being noticed?
intent: Physical network access is often overlooked. An unlabelled cable or an open, active network port can be an easy entry point for someone who gains physical access to your building.
examples: Cables clearly labelled and documented in a cable register
Network ports disabled in patch panels when not in use
Cable ducts locked or secured in shared or public areas
Regular physical audit of network ports and connections in server rooms

title: Equipment maintenance
description: Maintain equipment to ensure continued availability and integrity
question: Is the hardware that runs your service being maintained and serviced regularly — and does it get done by authorised people who log what they did?
intent: Unmaintained hardware fails unexpectedly. It also creates a security risk if unauthorised people service it and could install hardware implants or extract data from drives.
examples: Maintenance schedule for all servers and network equipment
Only vendor-authorised engineers allowed to service production hardware
Maintenance activity logged with who did what and when
Data cleared or equipment escorted when hardware goes off-site for repair

title: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment
description: Securely sanitise or destroy equipment before disposal or re-use
question: When hardware used by your service reaches end of life, is the data on it properly wiped or physically destroyed before it leaves your control?
intent: Simply deleting files or reinstalling an OS isn't enough — data can often be recovered from drives that haven't been properly sanitised. This is about ensuring data doesn't leave with the hardware.
examples: Certified data wiping to DoD or NIST standards before disposal or re-use
Physical shredding for drives containing highly sensitive data
Certificate of destruction obtained from disposal vendor and kept on file
Cloud provider data destruction confirmation when decommissioning cloud instances
Process documented and followed for every piece of decommissioned hardware

title: User endpoint devices
description: Protect user endpoint devices with policies and technical management controls
question: Do you know which laptops, phones, or other devices are used to access or manage your service — and are they all encrypted, patched, and managed by your organisation?
intent: Endpoints are the most common entry point for attackers. A stolen unencrypted laptop or an unpatched personal phone used for work email can compromise your entire service. This is about keeping control of the devices that touch your system.
examples: All devices enrolled in MDM/UEM (Intune, Jamf, etc.)
Full disk encryption enforced on all managed devices
Remote wipe capability tested annually
Only managed, organisation-approved devices allowed to connect to production systems
Separate work profile on mobile devices

title: Privileged access rights
description: Restrict, manage, and monitor privileged access accounts
question: Who has admin or elevated access to your service — and is that genuinely the smallest number of people who need it to do their job?
intent: Admin accounts are the keys to the kingdom. Every unnecessary admin account is a risk — if one gets compromised, the attacker immediately has admin-level access. Less is more here: the fewer admins, the smaller the attack surface.
examples: Named individual admin accounts (no shared "admin" credentials)
Just-in-time access for elevated privileges — access granted on request, revoked after use
PAM solution (CyberArk, BeyondTrust, AWS IAM Identity Center) for privileged session management
Admin actions logged and reviewed in SIEM
Regular review (quarterly) of who has admin access — remove anyone who doesn't need it

title: Information access restriction
description: Restrict access to information and functions based on the access control policy
question: Can everyone who can log in to your service see all the data in it — or is access limited to what each person or role actually needs?
intent: Not everyone needs to see everything. Fine-grained access controls reduce the damage if an account is compromised or if someone acts in bad faith — they can only access the data they were permitted to see.
examples: RBAC with clearly defined roles and no "see everything" default
Row-level security in databases (users only see records relevant to them)
Field-level masking for sensitive data (e.g. salary fields visible only to HR)
Multi-tenant isolation to prevent customers seeing each other's data
Access control verified as part of every major feature release

title: Access to source code
description: Restrict and control access to source code, dev tools, and software libraries
question: Is access to your service's source code limited to people who actively work on it — and do you know exactly who that is right now?
intent: Source code reveals how your application works and often exposes security weaknesses. Unrestricted access also means someone could insert malicious code or copy proprietary logic without you knowing.
examples: Repository access reviewed quarterly and revoked when developers leave the project
Branch protection rules requiring peer review before merging to main
Secrets scanning in your git pipeline to prevent credentials being committed
Code signing for production releases
No access for contractors beyond the duration of their engagement

title: Secure authentication
description: Implement secure authentication technologies and procedures for all access
question: Can anyone access your service with just a username and password — or do all users also need to verify with a second factor like an authenticator app?
intent: Passwords alone are no longer sufficient. Phishing, credential stuffing, and brute force attacks succeed constantly against password-only systems. MFA is one of the most effective controls available and relatively easy to implement.
examples: MFA enforced for all users, non-negotiable for admins
SSO using your corporate identity provider so access is centrally controlled
Account lockout after a configurable number of failed login attempts
Session timeout configured (users auto-logged out after inactivity)
No weak or default passwords — minimum complexity enforced at the system level

title: Capacity management
description: Monitor and manage resource capacity to ensure required system performance and availability
question: Do you monitor whether your service has enough compute, storage, and network capacity to keep running — and do you get an alert before it runs out?
intent: A system that runs out of disk space, gets overloaded, or hits a network bandwidth cap stops being available. Capacity management is as much about reliability and availability as it is about security.
examples: Cloud autoscaling configured to handle demand spikes
Alerts set at 80% thresholds for disk, memory, and CPU
Capacity reviewed as part of planning for major feature launches
Load testing performed before significant releases
Regular check on database size growth and estimated time to fill

title: Protection against malware
description: Implement malware detection, prevention, and recovery controls
question: Are the servers and endpoints used by your service protected against malware — and is that protection actively monitored and kept up to date?
intent: Even if you think your servers "don't need antivirus," modern threats like ransomware, cryptominers, and fileless malware target server workloads regularly. This is about having a detective control at the endpoint level.
examples: EDR/AV deployed on all endpoints and servers with auto-update enabled
Regular scheduled scans configured on all systems
Malware detection alerts forwarded to the SOC
Cloud workload protection enabled (e.g. AWS GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud, Crowdstrike Falcon)
Regular review of quarantined items and false positives

title: Management of technical vulnerabilities
description: Identify, evaluate, and remediate technical vulnerabilities in systems and software
question: Do you scan your service for known security vulnerabilities — and do you have a clear, realistic process for how quickly critical ones get fixed?
intent: New vulnerabilities in software are discovered every day. Without a process to find and fix them, your service gradually becomes easier to attack. This isn't about being perfect — it's about having a systematic way to stay ahead.
examples: Automated vulnerability scanning (Qualys, Tenable, AWS Inspector, or similar)
SLA for patching: critical vulns within 7 days, high within 30 days
Patch management calendar with assigned owners
Tracked remediation backlog in your ticketing system with regular review
Emergency patching process for actively exploited zero-days

title: Configuration management
description: Define, document, implement, and monitor configurations of hardware, software, and services
question: Is your service configured to a known-good security baseline — and do you get alerted if something changes unexpectedly from that baseline?
intent: Misconfiguration is one of the leading causes of cloud and system breaches. A configuration baseline gives you a known-good state and a way to detect when someone (or something) has drifted from it.
examples: CIS benchmark compliance checked for all production servers and cloud services
Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform, CloudFormation) for reproducible, auditable configuration
Config drift detection via AWS Config, Azure Policy, or similar tools
Hardened base images used for all new deployments
No manually configured production servers — changes go through IaC and code review

title: Information deletion
description: Delete information when it is no longer required, in line with retention requirements
question: When data in your service is no longer needed — because a retention period expired or a user asked for their data to be deleted — is it actually and completely deleted, not just hidden or deactivated?
intent: Data that should be deleted but isn't creates legal risk (especially under GDPR) and increases the potential impact of a breach. Soft deletes and archive flags aren't the same as deletion — this is about verifiable, complete removal.
examples: Automated data purge jobs that run after the defined retention period
Hard deletes in the database (not just a "deleted=true" flag) after retention expires
GDPR right-to-erasure workflow with documented completion
Deletion confirmed in audit logs with timestamp and record count
Backup data also purged after retention period ends, not kept indefinitely

title: Data masking
description: Mask data in line with access control policies, business rules, and legal requirements
question: If someone on your team needs to work with data from your production system for testing or support, are they working with real customer data — or is it masked or anonymised first?
intent: Sharing production data unnecessarily — especially PII — increases your exposure and creates legal risk. Masking lets people do their job with realistic-looking data without exposing real customer information.
examples: Dynamic data masking in SQL databases (e.g. only showing last 4 digits of a card number to support staff)
Anonymised or synthetic data sets generated for all non-production environments
Tokenisation for payment card data, replacing real values with tokens
Support dashboards that mask PII by default, with elevated access required to see full data

title: Data leakage prevention
description: Apply DLP controls to systems, networks, and devices to prevent sensitive data exfiltration
question: Is there anything actively stopping sensitive data from leaving your service through unexpected channels — like someone bulk-downloading a database and uploading it to a personal cloud storage account?
intent: Data exfiltration doesn't always look like a hack. Sometimes it's a well-intentioned employee doing the wrong thing, or an insider threat. DLP controls are a safety net that catches anomalous data movement before it becomes an incident.
examples: Blocking uploads to personal cloud drives (Dropbox, Google Drive) from corporate devices
Restrictions on bulk data exports from your application (rate limits, approval workflows)
Email DLP rules that flag large attachments containing PII
CASB solution for monitoring data flows to SaaS applications
Alerts on unusually large data transfers from production databases

title: Information backup
description: Maintain, test, and protect backup copies of information and systems
question: Do you have backups of your service's data — and have you actually tried restoring from them recently to confirm they work?
intent: A backup you've never tested is just hope. Backups only matter when something goes wrong, and that's the worst time to discover the restore process is broken. This is about treating backups as a capability you need to actively verify, not a checkbox.
examples: Daily automated backups with retention policy defined and enforced
Backup stored in a geographically separate location or cloud region
Restore test performed at least quarterly, with results documented
Backup access restricted (not everyone who can read production can read backups)
Backup data encrypted at rest and in transit

title: Redundancy of information processing facilities
description: Implement redundancy to meet system availability requirements
question: If a single server, database node, or key component in your service failed right now, would the service stay up — or would everything go down?
intent: Single points of failure are a risk to availability. Redundancy means the service keeps running even when individual components fail, which is especially important for services your business depends on.
examples: Active-active or active-passive database clusters
Load balancer with health checks removing unhealthy instances automatically
Multi-availability-zone deployment in your cloud environment
Auto-recovery configured on compute instances
Health checks integrated into Kubernetes or your container orchestration platform

title: Logging
description: Produce, store, protect, and analyse event logs from systems and applications
question: Does your service log who did what and when — and are those logs stored somewhere that even your own admins couldn't tamper with?
intent: Logs are your evidence trail. Without them, you can't investigate incidents, detect breaches, or prove compliance. Critically, logs must be protected from the people who administer the systems — otherwise they could be altered to cover tracks.
examples: Centralised log management or SIEM (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic)
Logs forwarded off the system immediately — not just stored locally where admins can delete them
Log retention of at least 12 months (at least 3 months hot, rest cold)
Logs include: user ID, action taken, timestamp, source IP, and outcome (success/failure)
Log access restricted to the security team, separate from system admin access

title: Monitoring activities
description: Monitor networks, systems, and applications for anomalous behaviour and potential threats
question: If someone were doing something suspicious in your service right now — brute-forcing logins, downloading unusually large amounts of data, accessing accounts at strange hours — would you know about it?
intent: Detecting threats in real time (or close to it) gives you a chance to respond before serious damage is done. Logging tells you what happened; monitoring tells you something is happening now.
examples: Logs forwarded to SIEM with correlation rules and alerts
Alert on failed login threshold being exceeded (e.g. 10 failures in 5 minutes)
Anomaly detection for unusual data access volumes or off-hours activity
Security dashboards visible to both the security team and the service owner team
Incident response playbook triggered when an alert fires

title: Clock synchronisation
description: Synchronise all system clocks to a single agreed time reference
question: Are all the components of your service synchronised to the same time source — so that when something goes wrong and you look at logs from different systems, the timestamps actually line up?
intent: Accurate timestamps are essential for incident investigation and log correlation. If your servers are out of sync by even a few minutes, correlating events across systems becomes extremely difficult — and in a fast-moving incident, those minutes matter.
examples: NTP client configured on all servers and containers, pointing to a reliable source
Clock drift monitored and alerted on
Container and pod time correctly inherited from host
Cloud instances using hypervisor-provided time synchronisation
NTP configuration verified as part of system hardening checklist

title: Use of privileged utility programs
description: Restrict and closely control the use of utility programs with administrative capabilities
question: Are tools like database admin consoles, OS-level shells, or network diagnostic tools restricted on your production systems — so that only the right people can use them, and every use is logged?
intent: Admin tools can bypass your normal application security controls. Someone with access to a database admin tool can query or modify data in ways your application would never allow. These tools need tighter controls than regular application access.
examples: Database admin consoles accessible only from a management bastion host, not directly from desktops
Admin tools requiring MFA and separate elevated credentials — not your everyday login
Every use of privileged tools logged to a tamper-proof audit trail
Admin tools not installed by default on production servers — installed on demand only
Session recording for high-risk admin tool use

title: Installation of software on operational systems
description: Control and restrict software installation on all operational and production systems
question: Could someone install unauthorised software on the servers or VMs running your service — and would you know about it if they did?
intent: Unauthorised software might be malicious or simply create unexpected vulnerabilities. In production environments, the software running should be exactly what you expect — no more, no less.
examples: Application whitelisting on production servers (only approved software can execute)
Package manager policies restricting to approved package repositories only
Infrastructure-as-Code and immutable infrastructure (no manual installs on running servers)
Alerts on unexpected new software or processes detected on production systems
Change management required before any new software is installed in production

title: Network security
description: Secure, manage, and control networks and network devices to protect systems
question: Does your service talk only to the systems and services it's supposed to — and is unnecessary network traffic actively blocked?
intent: Every open port and unrestricted network path is a potential attack route. The principle here is the same as access control: your service should communicate only with what it needs to, and nothing more.
examples: Firewall rules defined per service, explicitly allowing required traffic and denying everything else
Security groups and NSGs in cloud environments scoped to minimum required access
No production services exposed directly to the internet without a WAF or reverse proxy in front
Egress filtering in place (production systems can't call arbitrary external addresses)
Network topology diagram kept current and reviewed on change

title: Security of network services
description: Define and enforce security requirements for all network services
question: For each service your system connects to over the network — APIs, databases, message queues — are those connections secured, authenticated, and using current encryption standards?
intent: Service-to-service connections are an increasingly common attack vector, especially in microservices architectures. A compromised internal service that trusts unauthenticated connections from other internal services can quickly become a stepping stone to everything else.
examples: Mutual TLS (mTLS) between internal microservices
API keys and service accounts with minimal permissions and regular rotation
No internal services trusting connections without authentication ("trust nothing inside the network")
TLS 1.2 minimum enforced on all connections; TLS 1.3 preferred
Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) for zero-trust networking between services

title: Segregation of networks
description: Segregate networks to separate groups of services, users, and information systems
question: Is your production environment clearly separated from your development and test environments at the network level — so that a problem in one can't easily spread to another?
intent: Network segregation contains the blast radius of a breach or misconfiguration. If your dev environment is compromised, it shouldn't have a clear network path to your production database. Flat networks mean a single foothold can reach everything.
examples: Separate VPCs or VNets per environment (dev/test/prod) with no direct routing between them
Dedicated management network for admin access, isolated from production workload network
DMZ for any public-facing components, separated from internal services
Micro-segmentation within production to limit lateral movement
Firewall rules between segments that are regularly reviewed

title: Web filtering
description: Manage and restrict access to external websites to reduce exposure to web-based threats
question: Is outbound internet access from your service's systems restricted — so that if malware were present on one of those systems, it couldn't easily connect back to an attacker's infrastructure?
intent: Web filtering isn't just a productivity control — it stops malware from communicating with command-and-control servers and prevents systems from being redirected to malicious sites. Production servers especially should have tightly controlled outbound internet access.
examples: DNS filtering (Cisco Umbrella, Cloudflare Gateway) blocking known malicious domains
Proxy or egress filtering for outbound web traffic from production systems
Allowlist of known-good external domains for automated system calls (rather than "allow all")
Category-based blocking on endpoints (malware, phishing, file-sharing sites)
Alerts when production servers make unexpected outbound connections

title: Use of cryptography
description: Define and implement rules for the use of cryptography including key management
question: Is sensitive data in your service encrypted when it's stored and when it moves between systems — and do you know who holds the encryption keys and how they're managed?
intent: Encryption is only as good as your key management. If the data is encrypted but the key is sitting next to it in plaintext, or hardcoded in source code, or never rotated, the encryption provides false comfort.
examples: TLS 1.2+ enforced on all APIs and data transfer points
AES-256 encryption for all data at rest in databases and storage
Secrets and keys stored in a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) — not hardcoded
Key rotation schedule defined and automated where possible
No use of deprecated algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4) anywhere in the stack

title: Secure development life cycle
description: Establish and enforce rules for developing secure software and systems
question: Are security checks built into your development and release process — or does security only get looked at after something goes wrong?
intent: It's far cheaper to fix a security issue during design or development than after it's in production and potentially being exploited. This is about making security a normal part of how your team builds software, not an afterthought.
examples: Security requirements defined as part of user stories or acceptance criteria
Threat modelling workshop as part of design for new features or major changes
SAST tool (SonarQube, Semgrep, Checkmarx) integrated into your CI/CD pipeline
Security sign-off as part of your release checklist alongside testing and code review
Developer security training (OWASP Top 10, secure coding practices)

title: Application security requirements
description: Identify and approve information security requirements for all application development
question: Before building or changing a feature in your service, do you think through the security implications — what could go wrong and how to prevent it from the start?
intent: Security requirements need to be defined before development starts, not bolted on after. Catching a design flaw in a backlog conversation costs hours. Catching it after deployment and breach costs much more.
examples: Security user stories or acceptance criteria added to your backlog for all significant features
Threat modelling session for new features that handle sensitive data
OWASP Top 10 checklist consulted for any web-facing feature
Security review as part of design sign-off before implementation begins
Requirements covering authentication, authorisation, data validation, and error handling

title: Secure system architecture and engineering principles
description: Define and apply security engineering principles to design and build secure systems
question: Has your service's architecture been reviewed from a security angle — looking at where it could be attacked and how the design itself reduces those risks?
intent: Good security architecture decisions — where to put a WAF, how to segment the network, which trust boundaries exist — are much harder to retrofit than to build in from the start. Security should influence architecture, not just implementation.
examples: Threat model documented for the service (data flows, trust boundaries, attack surfaces)
Security architecture review with the security team before major design decisions are finalised
Least-privilege design for all inter-service communication
Defence-in-depth principle applied — no single control relied on as the only protection
Security architecture reviewed whenever there is a significant change to the system

title: Secure coding
description: Apply secure coding principles throughout software development to prevent common vulnerabilities
question: Are the developers working on your service following secure coding practices — and is there anything automatically checking the code for common vulnerabilities before it gets deployed?
intent: Many security vulnerabilities — SQL injection, cross-site scripting, insecure deserialisation — come from well-known, preventable coding mistakes. Automated tools catch these reliably before they reach production; relying only on manual review misses too much.
examples: SAST tool integrated into CI/CD pipeline and blocking merges on high/critical findings
Mandatory peer code review for all changes to production code
Developer training on OWASP Top 10 and common coding vulnerabilities
Dependency scanning to catch known CVEs in libraries (Dependabot, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check)
Secrets scanning in git hooks or CI pipeline to prevent credentials being committed

title: Security testing in development and acceptance
description: Define and perform security testing across development and acceptance stages
question: When did your service last have an independent security test — and were the findings actually fixed and verified?
intent: You can't fully rely on the development team to find their own security issues. Independent testing finds things internal teams miss — especially logic flaws, complex injection attacks, and issues that span multiple components.
examples: Annual penetration test by a qualified third party (CREST or equivalent certified tester)
DAST tool (OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite) run against the staging environment before each major release
Critical and high findings from tests must be resolved before release sign-off
All test findings tracked to closure with owner and due date
Bug bounty programme if the service is public-facing

title: Outsourced development
description: Supervise and monitor outsourced software development to maintain security standards
question: If third-party developers or a software vendor contribute code to your service, do you review what they deliver before it goes into production — rather than just trusting that it's secure?
intent: You remain responsible for the security of your service even if someone else wrote the code. External developers may not follow your standards, may not have been security-trained, or may have conflicting interests. You need to verify, not just trust.
examples: Code review process (including security-focused review) for all vendor-submitted code
Security requirements explicitly included in development contracts
SAST scans run on received code before acceptance
Penetration test or security assessment before accepting a major external release
Defined handover checklist including evidence of secure development practices

title: Separation of development, test and production environments
description: Separate development, test, and production environments to reduce security risk
question: Is your production environment clearly separated from your development and test environments — so a test deployment or a developer mistake can't accidentally affect real users or real data?
intent: Mixed environments are where accidents happen: a developer points a script at production thinking it's test, or test data overwrites production records. Separation makes these accidents much less likely and limits their blast radius.
examples: Separate cloud accounts or subscriptions per environment (dev / test / prod)
No production credentials or access stored in dev or test environments
Production data never used in test environments without masking or anonymisation
Separate CI/CD pipelines per environment with explicit promotion steps
Network isolation preventing dev/test systems from reaching production systems

title: Change management
description: Manage changes to IS, information systems, and processes using a formal process
question: When a change is made to your service — a config update, a new deployment, a firewall rule change — is there a record of what changed, who approved it, and how to roll it back if something goes wrong?
intent: Most incidents are caused or worsened by changes. A change management process provides visibility, accountability, and a safety net. Without it, when something breaks you often can't tell what changed or who to ask.
examples: Change tickets required for all production changes, including configuration updates
Peer review or CAB approval for significant or high-risk changes
Deployment pipeline with automated rollback capability or a tested manual rollback procedure
Post-deployment verification step to confirm the change had the intended effect
Emergency change process defined for urgent fixes, with post-implementation review

title: Test information
description: Select, protect, and manage test data to prevent misuse or exposure
question: If your service uses realistic data in its test environments, is that data anonymised — or could your less-secure test environment be exposing real customer information?
intent: Test environments are typically less secure than production — more people have access, security controls are looser, and they're often easier to breach. Yet they frequently contain copies of real data. This is a data breach waiting to happen.
examples: Automated data masking pipeline that generates anonymised test data from production
Synthetic data generation using tools like Faker, Mimesis, or a custom generator
Access controls on test environments comparable to production if real data must be used (though this is the last resort)
GDPR impact assessment for any use of real data in test
Test data refreshed on a schedule and deleted when no longer needed

title: Protection of information systems during audit testing
description: Plan and control audit testing activities to minimise disruption to operational systems
question: When an internal or external audit team needs access to your service, is that access time-limited, read-only where possible, logged — and does it not affect live users?
intent: Audit access needs to be meaningful enough to be useful, but not so broad that the audit itself creates risk or disruption. Poorly planned audit access can cause outages, expose sensitive data, or create additional attack surface.
examples: Dedicated read-only audit accounts scoped to relevant logs and configuration only
Agreed maintenance window for any active testing (e.g. pen tests against production)
On-call engineer notified and available during audit access windows
Audit activity logged separately and retained after the audit
Audit accounts created for the engagement and removed immediately after
